packs.title: Burlington’s lake, hills and legends
packs.promise: A stone clock, a 38-drawer filing cabinet, a lake-monster report and farms inside city limits.

q.s: Invent what’s inside a 38-drawer filing cabinet taller than a house.
st: From a public sidewalk, find it: steel filing drawers stacked more than 40 feet into the South End sky. Step back until you can see the very top drawer.
Count the drawers you can see. Artist Bren Alvarez gave it 38, one for each year a planned highway, the Southern Connector, had been waiting since it was first proposed in 1965.
Now label five drawers as if Burlington kept its own unfinished business in there: every sunset nobody photographed, a mitten lost in 1987, the parade that never got a permit. Make them yours.
Write your labels top drawer first, then circle the one drawer you’d open right now and say why.

q.t: Be the hand of the clock
q.s: Tell time with 14 granite stones and your own shadow.
st: Walk into the ring of 14 granite stones. The biggest weigh about 20 tons. Before you go further, notice which way the lake is.
Find the sundial at the center and stand on its date line. You are now the hand of the clock: your shadow points to the time.
Compare the time your shadow says with the time your phone says, then point out the stone that lines up best with the lake and the Adirondacks.
If shadow and phone disagree, make your best guess why. Daylight saving time is a good suspect. Try the shadow reading once more before you leave.

q.s: Watch the lake like a monster hunter, then write it up officially.
st: From the sand or shore, find a spot with open water and the Adirondacks in view. Settle in for ten patient minutes of lake watching.
Fill out your report: time, weather, wave height (flat, ripples or whitecaps) and anything that broke the surface, from a duck to a log to a very suspicious wave.
Rate each sighting on the Champ scale, from 1 (definitely a duck) to 5 (I’m telling my grandkids). Sketch your top candidate.
Sign and date it. People have been reporting something in this lake since at least 1819, so you’re in good company.

packs.title: Burlington’s Church Street and waterfront
packs.promise: Two walkable afternoons from brick Church Street down the hill to the lake’s sunset swings.

q.t: The small stages of Church Street
q.s: Collect five tiny performances along four brick blocks.
st: Walk the four brick blocks slowly, top to bottom, and treat everything as a show.

Collect five small stages: a musician or performer (or the empty spot where one would stand), a dog doing something important, a shop window arranged like a scene, someone reading in public and one surprise of your own.
Brave bonus (optional): tell a performer or shopkeeper the one thing that made you stop. You never have to tip or buy anything.
Write your five stages as a playbill, with a title, cast and one-line review for each.

q.s: Stack book spines into a poem inside a Carnegie library.
st: Browsing is free and doesn’t require a library card. Head into the stacks with one rule: you’re shopping for titles, not books.
Pick three to five books whose spine titles, read top to bottom, make a tiny poem about Burlington, today or you.
Stack them quietly at a table and read the poem from top to bottom, with the authors as your band. Swap the order once and choose the version you like best.
Leave the books on a reshelving cart or wherever staff ask. Don’t reshelve them yourself.

q.s: Claim a boardwalk swing and give the lake five quiet minutes.
st: Find a swing on the boardwalk facing the lake. If they’re all taken, wait nearby for one to open up, or don’t.
Swing gently for five minutes with your phone away. Watch the Adirondacks, the water and the light.
Afterward, bring back three colors you saw and one sound that was there the whole time. Say them to a friend or keep them in your head. Your phone can stay away.
